status.label: Design ready — needs approval
status.detail: The WinUI 3 Quick Accent regression is bounded, reproducible, and already tied to the migrated selector layout. The repository files and verification plan are specific enough for implementation review.

next_action.label: Approve the detailed design
next_action.reason: Repository files, implementation steps, and verification are specific enough to start the fork-side fix when desired.

design.root_cause: The WinUI 3 Quick Accent selector still expects horizontal overflow, but the migrated list explicitly hides its horizontal scrollbar and the overlay height is hard-coded for a single row of accent cells. When all languages overflow the viewport, users can scroll the hidden list, but the UI never exposes the scrollbar affordance that the WPF version showed.
evidence: Issue #49454 includes concrete steps, side-by-side screenshots, and an explicit regression note that the WPF version still showed the scrollbar.

`src/modules/poweraccent/PowerAccent.UI/PowerAccentXAML/SelectorControl.xaml` sets `ScrollViewer.HorizontalScrollBarVisibility="Hidden"` while keeping horizontal scrolling enabled on `CharactersList`.
`src/modules/poweraccent/PowerAccent.UI/PowerAccentXAML/MainWindow.xaml.cs` sizes the overlay with a fixed `RowHeightDip` and never adds scrollbar height when the accent list overflows.

`src/modules/poweraccent/PowerAccent.Core/Tools/Calculation.cs` already clamps toolbar width to the display and relies on scrolling once the accent list is wider than the allowed viewport, so overflow is an intended steady state.

affected_files.purpose: Defines the Quick Accent character list and currently suppresses the horizontal scrollbar even when overflow occurs.
Measures accent-list content width and should expose overflow-aware viewport or scrollbar metrics to the window sizing code.
Sizes and positions the Quick Accent overlay and currently assumes the selector is always a fixed-height single row.
Holds the testable toolbar size math and is the right place to add overflow-aware height calculations.
Provides focused regression coverage for toolbar geometry and should gain overflow-height tests.

implementation_steps.current_behavior: The accent list scrolls horizontally, but `CharactersList` forces `ScrollViewer.HorizontalScrollBarVisibility="Hidden"`, so users never see the scrollbar even when content extends beyond the viewport.
implementation_steps.change: Switch the list to overflow-aware scrollbar visibility and expose whether the realized list currently needs that scrollbar.
edge_cases: Do not show the scrollbar when the selected language set fits inside the available width.
Keep vertical scrolling disabled so the one-row accent bar still behaves like a transient keyboard overlay.
Retain the existing selected-item behavior and no-animation policy.
tests: Manual repro for issue #49454 with “All languages” selected on a narrow display should visibly show a horizontal scrollbar.
A wide display that does not overflow should still render without a scrollbar.

implementation_steps.current_behavior: Toolbar width is testable, but toolbar height remains implicit in `MainWindow` and cannot describe the extra vertical space a visible horizontal scrollbar needs.
implementation_steps.change: Introduce a pure helper that returns the overflow-dependent toolbar height (base row + optional description row + optional scrollbar allowance), then cover it in `CalculationTests`.
edge_cases: Treat zero or non-finite scrollbar measurements as “no extra height” to avoid layout exceptions before the list is realized.
Keep the existing width-clamp behavior unchanged; only the vertical size should grow when overflow is present.
Cover both description-row and no-description-row combinations in tests.
tests: Add data-driven `CalculationTests` cases for no overflow, overflow without description, and overflow with description.
Retain the existing `GetToolbarWidth` regression coverage unchanged.

implementation_steps.current_behavior: After layout, `MainWindow` measures width and then resizes the overlay with a constant one-row height, so even if the list could surface a scrollbar there is no reserved space for it.
implementation_steps.change: After `Selector.UpdateLayout()`, read the selector's overflow metrics, compute the overflow-aware height through the new `Calculation` helper, and size the overlay before `Reveal()` so the scrollbar is visible in the first painted frame.
edge_cases: DPI scaling must continue to round outward so the scrollbar is not clipped on fractional-scale displays.
The description row still needs to appear below the characters when Unicode descriptions are enabled.
The overlay should not jump between frames: overflow state must be measured before `Reveal()`.
tests: Build `PowerAccent.UI` and manually verify the scrollbar appears on the first summon with all languages enabled.
Regression-check that narrow language sets still center correctly and keep the previous height.

verify: Build the UI project: `pwsh .\tools\build\build.ps1 -Platform x64 -Configuration Debug -Path .\src\modules\poweraccent\PowerAccent.UI\PowerAccent.UI.csproj`

Build and run the geometry tests: `pwsh .\tools\build\build.ps1 -Platform x64 -Configuration Debug -Path .\src\modules\poweraccent\PowerAccent.Core.UnitTests\PowerAccent.Core.UnitTests.csproj`, then run the `CalculationTests` suite with VS Test Explorer or `vstest.console.exe`.
Launch a Debug PowerToys build, enable Quick Accent, select “All languages”, narrow the available screen width, press `E`, and confirm a horizontal scrollbar is visible beneath the characters.
Repeat on a wide display and confirm no unnecessary scrollbar appears when the list fits.
Toggle Unicode descriptions on and confirm the description row still renders below the character list without clipping the scrollbar.
risks: Adding scrollbar height changes the popup footprint and may slightly shift the overlay on very small displays.
ScrollViewer template differences across Windows App SDK versions could change the realized scrollbar thickness, so the code must tolerate missing or delayed metrics.
Always-visible scrollbar space would be a visual regression; the fix must stay overflow-aware.
alternatives: Widening the popup instead of showing a scrollbar would break the existing width clamp and can push the overlay off-screen on smaller displays.
Adding fade gradients without a scrollbar would still hide the exact overflow extent that users asked for.
Paginating accent characters would be a larger UX change than restoring the WPF-era scrollbar behavior.
